practiceProblems.title: Advanced plotting techniques
practiceProblems.description:
Advanced Plotting Techniques will cover Multiple plots in further detail along with fancy plot types such as Boxplots and Heatmaps.

In this module - we will also introduce time series plots and 3D plots. However, we will keep our examples and content beginner friendly so that you get working knowledge of these techniques as a beginner.

This code creates a 3D scatter plot representing customer segmentation. Here's a breakdown of what it does and its marketing relevance:
- We generate sample data for 100 customers with three attributes:
   - Age: randomly distributed between 20 and 70
   - Income: randomly distributed between $20,000 and $100,000
   - Purchase Frequency: randomly distributed between 1 and 20 purchases per year
- Business Relevance:
   - Customer Visualization: This plot provides a quick visual representation of your customer base across three important dimensions.
   - Identifying Patterns: Even with this simple plot, you can start to see patterns or clusters in your customer data.
   - Outlier Detection: Unusual customers (e.g., young customers with high income and high purchase frequency) will stand out in this 3D space.

Again - do not worry about the specific code - we will learn some of these basics in the current module.

practiceProblems.title: Subplots
practiceProblems.description:
We completed an example on subplots in the previous module. Let us revisit subplots in the current module as well.

Subplots allow you to create multiple plots within a single figure. This is useful for comparing different datasets or showing various aspects of the same data.

We have populated the subplot code in the IDE - it is a slight variant of what we learnt in the previous module. Let us understand this code better
- fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 4))
   - This line creates a figure with two subplots side by side
   - plt.subplots(1, 2) creates 1 row and 2 columns of subplots
   - (ax1, ax2) are Axes objects, representing each subplot. We get two because we specified 2 columns
- ax1.plot(x, np.sin(x)) - ax1 refers to the first subplot
- ax2.plot(x, np.cos(x)) - ax2 refers to the second subplot

### Task
Create a figure with 3 subplots arranged vertically. \
Plot y = x, y = x^2, and y = x^3 for x values from 0 to 5 in the three subplots respectively. \
You can name each subplot as per your choice.

practiceProblems.title: Grid Layouts
practiceProblems.description:
Grid layouts allow for more complex arrangements of subplots. \
You can create grids of different sizes and shapes to organize your plots effectively.

Notice the difference in the syntax of `fig, axs = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(6, 6))` as compared to the previous problem.
- The return values fig, axs:
   - fig is the Figure object. It represents the entire figure (all subplots together)
   - axs is a 2D numpy array of Axes objects. Each Axes object represents one subplot
- The arguments (2, 2) creates a 2x2 grid, resulting in 4 subplots total.

### Task
Create a 2x3 grid of subplots. \
In each subplot, plot a different trigonometric function (sin, cos, tan, arcsin, arccos, arctan) for x values from -π to π. \
Label each subplot with the appropriate function name.

practiceProblems.title: Sharing Axes
practiceProblems.description:
Sharing axes between subplots is useful when you want to align the scales of multiple plots for easier comparison. You can share x-axes, y-axes, or both.

To achieve this, we use sharex and sharey parameters in plt.subplots():
```python
fig, (ax1, ax2) = plt.subplots(2, 1, sharex=True)
```

Considerations
- When sharing axes, you typically only need to set labels on one of the shared axes.
- You can still customize individual plots (e.g., different y-axis scales) while sharing the x-axis.

Check out the code in the IDE.

### Task
Create two subplots arranged horizontally. \
In the left subplot, plot y = x^2, and in the right subplot, plot y = x^3. \
Share the y-axis between the two plots. \
Use different colors for each plot.

practiceProblems.title: Advanced plot types
practiceProblems.description:
In this topic, lets look at some Fancy plot types such as 
- Create and interpret pie charts
- Understand and generate box plots
- Produce and analyze violin plots
- Create and interpret heatmaps

Run the project on the right - This heatmap visualizes sales performance across different products and regions for a company. It's a common scenario in business analytics where managers need to quickly identify patterns, strengths, and weaknesses in their sales data. What the Heatmap Displays:
- Products and Regions:
  - The y-axis shows different products (Laptops, Smartphones, Tablets, Smartwatches).
  - The x-axis represents different regions (North, South, East, West, Central).
- Sales Volume:
  - Each cell in the heatmap represents the sales volume for a specific product in a specific region.
  - The color intensity indicates the sales volume - darker colors (more red) represent higher sales, while lighter colors (more yellow) represent lower sales.

Key Insights from This Visualization:
- Product Performance: You can quickly see which products are performing best overall by looking at the rows with the most intense colors.
- Regional Trends: The columns show how different regions are performing, allowing you to identify strong and weak markets.

Let us learn some of these basics in the current topic.

practiceProblems.title: Pie chart
practiceProblems.description:
Pie charts display data as slices of a circular graph, where each slice represents a category's proportion of the whole.

Run the code in the IDE. This is how the code works
- plt.pie() function - This function creates the pie chart. Here's what each parameter does:
   - sizes: This is a list or array of numerical values that determine the size of each slice in the pie.
   - labels=categories: This assigns labels to each slice. Categories should be a list of strings corresponding to each value in sizes.
   - autopct='%1.1f%%': This adds percentage labels on the slices. %1.1f formats the number to one decimal place. %% adds a percent sign after the number.
   - startangle=90: This rotates the start of the pie by 90 degrees counterclockwise. By default, the first slice starts at the x-axis.
- plt.axis('equal') - This line ensures that the pie chart is drawn as a perfect circle. Without this, the pie might be drawn as an ellipse depending on the plot's aspect ratio.

### Task
Create a pie chart showing the distribution of expenses in a monthly budget (e.g., rent, food, utilities, entertainment). Use the following values
```python
expenses = ['Rent', 'Food', 'Utilities', 'Entertainment']
amounts = [1200, 400, 200, 200]
colors = ['#ff9999', '#66b3ff', '#99ff99', '#ffcc99']
```

practiceProblems.title: Violin Plots
practiceProblems.description:
Violin plots are similar to box plots but show the full distribution of the data. The width of each "violin" represents the frequency of data points. They're especially helpful for visualising the distribution of data across different categories or groups.

The resulting plot will show three violins side by side, each representing the distribution of one of the groups:
- The first violin (leftmost) represents group1: a normal distribution centered around 100 with a relatively small spread.
- The second violin represents group2: a normal distribution centered around 80 with a larger spread.
- The third violin (rightmost) represents group3: a gamma distribution, which is asymmetric and skewed to the right.

practiceProblems.title: Heat maps
practiceProblems.description:
Heatmaps display data in a 2D grid using colors to represent values. \
They're useful for showing patterns or correlations in complex datasets.

Check out the code given in the IDE. Some add-ons as compared to what we have learnt earlier
- Creating the heatmap:
   - plt.figure(figsize=(8, 6)) sets the figure size
   - plt.imshow(data, cmap='viridis') is the main function for creating the heatmap 
      - data is our input array
      - cmap='viridis' sets the color scheme (a blue-green-yellow colormap)
- Adding a colorbar
   - plt.colorbar() adds a colorbar to show the scale

### Task
Use the following monthly temperatures for 3 years to generate the corresponding heatmap.
```python
monthly_temps = [
    [5, 10, 15, 20, 25, 30, 32, 31, 26, 21, 15, 8],  # Year 2020
    [6, 11, 16, 21, 26, 31, 33, 32, 27, 22, 16, 9],  # Year 2021
    [4, 9, 14, 19, 24, 29, 31, 30, 25, 20, 14, 7]    # Year 2022
]
```

practiceProblems.title: Working with Time Series Data
practiceProblems.description:
We're working with daily temperature data for a city over the course of a year. This is a common scenario in meteorology, climate science, and urban planning, where understanding temperature trends is crucial.

This example demonstrates several key concepts in working with time series data:
- Data preparation and indexing with dates
- Handling daily data
- Calculating rolling statistics (moving average)
- Visualizing time series data
- Extracting insights from the data (e.g., extreme values, basic statistics)

When you run this code, you'll get a visualization that shows the daily temperature fluctuations along with a smoother trend line (the moving average). This kind of visualization is very useful for identifying patterns, trends, and anomalies in the data.

We will learn some of the basic visualisation techniques for time-series data in our current topic.

practiceProblems.title: Handling Missing Data
practiceProblems.description:
Real-world time series data often contains missing values. \
We need to handle these appropriately before plotting.

Here, we use our understanding of NaN values in Pandas and the data cleaning techniques that we learnt earlier to handle the data before plotting.
```python
# Assuming df has some NaN values
df_cleaned = df.dropna()  # Remove rows with NaN values

# Or, fill NaN values with a method like forward fill
df_filled = df.fillna(method='ffill')
```

### Task

You need to create two plots: one where the missing values are dropped, and another where they're filled using forward fill.

practiceProblems.title: Resampling Time Series Data
practiceProblems.description:
Resampling is the process of changing the frequency of your time series data.
- It can involve either upsampling (increasing frequency) or downsampling (decreasing frequency).
- Common use cases include aggregating high-frequency data to a lower frequency (e.g., hourly to daily) or filling in missing data points in low-frequency data.

Resampling is performed using the resample() function in Pandas for time series data.

Resampling can significantly affect how your data looks when plotted. \
It can reveal trends that might be obscured in high-frequency data.

Run the code given in the IDE. Observe the following
- We created a time series of hourly sales data.
- We then resampled this data to daily and weekly frequencies.
- For each of these, we plotted the sales values over time.

These plots show how the sales values change over time at different granularities, but they don't show the distribution of the sales values themselves.

practiceProblems.title: Creating 3D Axes
practiceProblems.description:
In Matplotlib, 3D plotting is done using the Axes3D object from the mpl_toolkits.mplot3d module. \
This object allows us to create a 3D coordinate system where we can plot our data.

Adding a 3D subplot:
- We add a 3D subplot to our figure using fig.add_subplot().
- The 111 argument means we're creating a 1x1 grid of subplots, and this is the first subplot.
- The projection='3d' argument is crucial - it tells Matplotlib we want a 3D axes.
- We use set_xlabel(), set_ylabel(), and set_zlabel() to label each axis.

Check the code in the IDE, we have plotted 10 random coordinates.

### Task
Create a 3D axes with the following specifications:
- Set the figure size to 12x10 inches.
- Label the axes as 'Time', 'Distance', and 'Speed'.
- Set the viewing angle to elevation 30 and azimuth 60.
- Add a title "Vehicle Motion in 3D".
- Add 20 random points colored in blue.

practiceProblems.title: 3D Scatter Plots
practiceProblems.description:
3D scatter plots display data points in three-dimensional space. \
Each point represents a single data item with three values: x, y, and z coordinates. These plots are useful for visualizing relationships between three variables simultaneously.

For a scatter plot, we need three arrays of equal length for x, y, and z coordinates.

We use the scatter() function of our 3D axes object to create the scatter plot. The basic syntax is ax.scatter(x, y, z), where x, y, and z are our data arrays. We can customize various aspects of the scatter plot:
- c: Color of the points (can be a single color or an array for color-coding)
- s: Size of the points
- alpha: Transparency of the points
- cmap: Colormap (when color-coding points)

### Task
Create a 3D scatter plot with the following specifications:
- Generate 500 points where:
  - x values are random numbers between 0 and 10
  - y values are the square root of x
  - z values are the logarithm of x
- Color-code the points based on their z-values.

practiceProblems.title: 3D Surface Plots
practiceProblems.description:
3D surface plots are used to visualize a function of two variables, f(x, y). \
They create a surface in 3D space where the height of the surface represents the value of the function. \
These plots are useful for visualizing mathematical functions, terrain data, or any 2D grid of values.

We need to create a grid of x and y values using np.meshgrid(). \
We use the plot_surface() function of our 3D axes object to create the surface plot. \
The basic syntax is ax.plot_surface(X, Y, Z), where X, Y are 2D arrays from meshgrid, and Z is our calculated function values.

Run the code given in the IDE to view the output.

### Task
Create a 3D surface plot with the following specifications:
- Plot the function f(x, y) = x*exp(-x^2 - y^2) for x and y ranging from -2 to 2.
- Use a custom colormap (e.g., 'coolwarm')
